description: COVID-19 equity crash pushed the equity share of the actual benchmark index to 65.8% at month-end March 2020, 4.2 percentage points below the 70% strategic weight -- past the -2pp band. This triggered a rebalancing. NBIM states explicitly this was 'the first [rebalancing] to have been carried out under the new rebalancing regime introduced in 2019', i.e. no crossing occurred between 1 May 2019 and March 2020.

Equity share was back at the 70% strategic weight by the end of Q2 2020, following gradual rebalancing purchases of equities plus the effect of the market rebound and government withdrawals over the same period.

description: Most recent published data point (from the live 'Benchmark index' page, not yet superseded by a year-end archive entry): actual-benchmark-index equity share of 72.93%, 0.93pp past the 72.00% trigger -- the largest overshoot on this measure since the archive resumes reporting it in 2022. Fund-level equity share at the same date was 72.1% (right at the edge of its own 72% reference point, but that is not the metric the rule uses). No rebalancing narrative found in the Half-year Report 2026.

Confirmed, NBIM-narrated band crossings since the 70%/2pp regime took effect (1 May 2019): ONE (March-June 2020, COVID). Additional apparent breaches on the exact rule metric (actual benchmark index, not fund-level) are visible in year-end/current snapshots for 2024, 2025 and mid-2026, cumulating roughly 2 years of the metric sitting above the trigger line, but NBIM's own reports do not narrate a discrete 'rebalancing' event for this period -- most likely because gradual rebalancing (adopted in 2019 specifically to avoid abrupt trades) makes a slow, modest, sub-1pp overshoot invisible in prose even if small offsetting trades are happening every month. 2020H2-2021 cannot be checked at all because NBIM's own archive is blank for those two year-ends. Net: this is NOT a 'two or three times in the fund's history' story on the OLD 4pp rule, nor a 'never' story on the new 2pp rule -- it looks more like 'one dramatic, explicitly documented crossing (2020), plus a persistent, undocumented, small overshoot from sometime in 2024 to the most recent data (mid-2026)'.
